metadata.title: Summary Benchmarks for the Academy’s Preferred Practice Pattern® Guidelines
quality_flags: A section heading for glaucoma suspect evaluation is incomplete.
The laser trabeculoplasty section also uses the term laser trabeculectomy.
metadata.summary: These summary benchmarks address evaluation, treatment, follow-up, and patient education for primary open-angle glaucoma, glaucoma suspects, and primary angle-closure disease. They outline medical, laser, and incisional approaches, including perioperative care. The guidance describes how evidence and recommendations are rated while emphasizing that care must be adapted to individual patients.

target_population: Patients undergoing glaucoma surgery or iridotomy

prevention: Use topical ocular hypotensive agents around the time of surgery, particularly in patients with severe disease.
Measure IOP immediately before surgery and within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward.

recognition: Evidence that the bleb is failing

management.actions: Arrange more frequent postoperative visits as needed.

Use additional measures as needed to improve aqueous flow into the bleb and reduce IOP, including injection of antifibrotic agents, bleb massage, suture adjustment, release or lysis, or bleb needling.

recognition: Flat or shallow anterior chamber after surgery

management.actions: Increase the frequency of postoperative visits as needed; a flat anterior chamber may require reformation.
Repair the leak when it develops.
Instruct the patient to notify the ophthalmologist immediately if these symptoms and signs occur.

prevention: Explain that the risk persists for the patient's lifetime after filtration surgery.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Iridotomy may be considered to reduce the risk of developing angle closure.
Schedule an iridotomy for the fellow eye when its chamber angle is anatomically narrow; approximately half of fellow eyes can develop AACC within 5 years.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients whose fellow eye has an anatomically narrow chamber angle

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use topical ocular hypotensive agents around iridotomy to prevent sudden IOP elevation, particularly when disease is severe.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing iridotomy, particularly those with severe disease

prophylaxis.recommendation: Teach eyelid closure or nasolacrimal occlusion after applying topical medication to reduce systemic absorption.

infection_management.prevention: Advise patients that filtration surgery carries a lifelong risk of endophthalmitis.
infection_management.management: Instruct patients to contact their ophthalmologist immediately if pain and decreased vision occur with redness and discharge.

therapies_index.name: medical therapy
approved_indications: Lowering IOP in patients with POAG when treatment is indicated.
Lowering IOP in glaucoma suspects when treatment is indicated.
Initially lowering IOP during AACC to relieve pain and clear corneal edema before iridotomy.
Ongoing IOP reduction after iridotomy if IOP remains elevated long term and PAC or PACG develops.
monitoring: Assess whether the desired IOP reduction is achieved.
Review adherence when damage progresses despite achievement of the target IOP.

therapies_index.name: glaucoma medication
approved_indications: Medical treatment of glaucoma.
key_toxicities: Local ocular and systemic adverse effects or toxicity.
monitoring: Assess local ocular and systemic adverse effects or toxicity.
Review medication use, including the time of the last administration.

therapies_index.name: topical ocular hypotensive agents
approved_indications: Reducing IOP in treated patients.
Preventing a sudden IOP rise around iridotomy, particularly in patients with severe disease.
therapies_index.administration: Topical ocular administration; no dosing schedule is specified.
monitoring: Monitor IOP.
A carefully monitored reduction in treatment may be appropriate after prolonged optic nerve stability with low IOP.

therapies_index.name: parasympathomimetic
approved_indications: May be considered before LPI to facilitate the procedure.
therapies_index.administration: Consider preoperative use; no route or dose is specified.

therapies_index.name: topical corticosteroids
approved_indications: Postoperative treatment after incisional glaucoma surgery.
Postoperative treatment after iridotomy.
therapies_index.administration: Topical administration after surgery; no dose or duration is specified.

therapies_index.name: antifibrotic agents
approved_indications: An injection may be used if bleb failure develops after incisional glaucoma surgery, as part of treatment to improve aqueous flow into the bleb and lower IOP.
therapies_index.administration: Injection; no dose or schedule is specified.
monitoring: Assess the bleb for evidence of failure and monitor IOP.

therapies_index.name: laser trabeculoplasty
approved_indications: May be used as initial or adjunctive treatment for POAG.
monitoring: Check IOP at least once immediately before surgery and within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward.
Examine the patient within 6 weeks after surgery, or earlier if IOP-related optic nerve injury is a concern.

therapies_index.name: Laser trabeculectomy
approved_indications: The document describes this procedure as effective for lowering IOP.
therapies_index.administration: May be performed over 180 degrees or 360 degrees of the angle.

therapies_index.name: incisional glaucoma surgery
approved_indications: An option for lowering IOP, alone or combined with other treatment.
key_toxicities: Postoperative complications described include a flat or shallow anterior chamber, early bleb failure, increased inflammation, and Tenon's cyst.
monitoring: Evaluate visual acuity, IOP, and the anterior segment on the first postoperative day and at least once during the first 1 to 2 weeks.
If there are no complications, make additional visits during a 3-month period to assess visual acuity, IOP, and the anterior segment.
Arrange more frequent visits when postoperative complications occur.

therapies_index.name: trabecular meshwork/Schlemm's canal-based MIGS
monitoring: Perform gonioscopy before surgery, particularly when this procedure is being considered.

therapies_index.name: filtration surgery
key_toxicities: A lifelong risk of endophthalmitis is described.
monitoring: Instruct patients to contact their ophthalmologist immediately if pain and reduced vision occur with redness and discharge.

therapies_index.name: bleb massage
approved_indications: May be used if bleb failure develops after incisional glaucoma surgery to improve aqueous flow into the bleb and lower IOP.
monitoring: Assess for bleb failure and monitor IOP.

therapies_index.name: suture adjustment
approved_indications: May be used if bleb failure develops after incisional glaucoma surgery to improve aqueous flow into the bleb and lower IOP.
monitoring: Assess for bleb failure and monitor IOP.

therapies_index.name: suture release or lysis
approved_indications: May be used if bleb failure develops after incisional glaucoma surgery to improve aqueous flow into the bleb and lower IOP.
monitoring: Assess for bleb failure and monitor IOP.

therapies_index.name: bleb needling
approved_indications: May be used if bleb failure develops after incisional glaucoma surgery to improve aqueous flow into the bleb and lower IOP.
monitoring: Assess for bleb failure and monitor IOP.

therapies_index.name: repair of bleb leak
approved_indications: Treatment of a postoperative bleb leak when it develops.

therapies_index.name: reformation of a flat anterior chamber
approved_indications: Treatment of a flat anterior chamber when it develops after surgery.

therapies_index.name: Laser iridotomy
approved_indications: Preferred surgical treatment for AACC, to be performed as soon as possible after initial medical lowering of IOP.
May be considered for PACS to reduce the risk of developing angle closure.
Prophylactic treatment of a fellow eye with an anatomically narrow chamber angle.
therapies_index.administration: Enlarge the opening when needed to attain a diameter of at least 100 microns.
monitoring: Check IOP at least once immediately before the procedure and within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward.
Confirm patency by directly observing aqueous fluid and pigment moving from the posterior to the anterior chamber; a red reflex alone does not establish patency.
At follow-up, confirm patency by viewing the zonules, anterior lens capsule, or ciliary processes, and measure IOP.
If not done immediately after iridotomy, perform dark-room gonioscopy with compression or indentation to assess the extent of PAS.
Examine the fundus when clinically indicated.

therapies_index.name: cyclophotocoagulation
therapies_index.administration: Selection instead of other procedures is left to the treating ophthalmologist in consultation with the patient.

therapies_index.name: iridoplasty
therapies_index.administration: For plateau iris, the decision between observation and treatment is left to the ophthalmologist because evidence supporting prophylactic use is not convincing.

therapies_index.name: eyelid closure
therapies_index.mechanism: Reduces systemic absorption after topical medication application.
approved_indications: Patient education when topical glaucoma medication is applied.
therapies_index.administration: Close the eyelids after applying topical medication.

therapies_index.name: nasolacrimal occlusion
therapies_index.mechanism: Reduces systemic absorption after topical medication application.
approved_indications: Patient education when topical glaucoma medication is applied.

therapies_index.name: vision rehabilitation
approved_indications: Patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness may be referred and encouraged to use appropriate services.

therapies_index.name: keratorefractive surgery
key_toxicities: Laser vision correction may reduce contrast sensitivity and decrease the accuracy of IOP measurements.
monitoring: Inform patients considering the procedure about its possible effect on the accuracy of IOP measurements.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Document ocular history, including refractive error, trauma and prior surgery; race/ethnicity; family and systemic history; relevant records; current medications; and previous glaucoma laser or incisional surgery.
Assess pressure relative to the individualized target and identify changes during follow-up.
Examine the anterior chamber angle.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial examination and periodically thereafter; also when an angle-closure component, anterior chamber shallowing, an angle abnormality or an unexplained IOP change is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.test: Optic nerve head (ONH) and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess optic nerve and RNFL status and detect progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial examination; reassess the ONH during follow-up.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess functional stability or progression.
Assess structural status and changes over time.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial diagnostic testing; imaging changes may inform subsequent target-pressure adjustment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Review interval ocular and systemic history, ocular-medication adverse effects, relevant medication use and the time of the last administration.

follow_up.schedule: The consensus-based maximum interval between evaluations is 6 months when target IOP is achieved, damage has not progressed and control has lasted ≤6 months; 12 months when those conditions hold and control has lasted >6 months; 1–2 months when damage is progressing, regardless of whether target IOP has been achieved; and 3–6 months when target IOP has not been achieved but damage is not progressing. More advanced damage or greater lifetime risk may warrant shorter intervals.
recommended_tests: Review interval ocular and systemic history, medication adverse effects, medication use and timing of the last dose.
Measure visual acuity and IOP, and perform slit-lamp biomicroscopy.
Reassess the ONH and visual fields.
Perform gonioscopy periodically and when an angle-closure component, anterior chamber shallowing, angle abnormality or unexplained IOP change is suspected.
long_term_effects: Assess local ocular and systemic adverse effects and toxicity in patients using glaucoma medication.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Discuss the possibility of lifelong treatment. Patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness may be referred to vision rehabilitation and social services.

conditions.name: glaucoma suspect
conditions.description: The document discusses monitoring for progression to POAG through changes in optic-disc or retinal structure and visual-field function.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Record ocular history, including refractive error, trauma and prior ocular surgery; race/ethnicity; family and systemic history; relevant records; current and previous ocular and nonocular medications; and prior cataract surgery, LASIK or incisional surgery.
Monitor pressure and its response to treatment, if given.
Assess the anterior chamber angle.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial examination and during follow-up if an angle-closure component, chamber shallowing, an angle abnormality or an unexplained IOP change is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.test: Optic nerve head (ONH) and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess structural findings.
Assess functional changes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial diagnostic testing; repeat testing is preferable if glaucomatous visual-field damage is newly identified.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A newly detected glaucomatous visual-field finding should be checked with repeat testing.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess structural findings alongside perimetric and other structural information when making management decisions.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Digital imaging should be considered together with perimetric and other structural information.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Review interval ocular and systemic medical history and medications; for treated patients, assess ocular-medication adverse effects, medication use and the time of the last administration.

recommended_tests: Review interval ocular and systemic medical history and medication use.
For treated patients, review ocular-medication adverse effects and the time of the last administration.
Measure visual acuity and IOP, and perform slit-lamp biomicroscopy.
Perform gonioscopy if an angle-closure component, anterior chamber shallowing, an angle abnormality or an unexplained IOP change is suspected.
Monitor optic-disc and retinal structure and visual-field function for progression to POAG.
long_term_effects: Review adverse effects of ocular medication in treated patients.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Discuss risk factors, prognosis, life expectancy and the possibility that treatment, once begun, may continue long term. Patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness may be referred to vision rehabilitation and social services.

conditions.name: Primary Angle-Closure Disease
conditions.clinical_presentation: The initial history considers blurred vision, halos around lights, ocular pain, headache and ocular redness. Examination may reveal a shallow central or peripheral anterior chamber, conjunctival hyperemia or corneal swelling in acute cases, signs of anterior chamber inflammation, iris abnormalities, lens changes or corneal endothelial cell loss. A small corneal diameter indicates a smaller eye at greater risk for PACD.

subtypes.name: acute angle-closure crisis (AACC)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The document describes acute findings that can include conjunctival hyperemia and corneal swelling; anterior chamber inflammation or a mid-dilated pupil can suggest a current or recent attack.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Ask about blurred vision, halos around lights, ocular pain, headache and redness; family history of acute angle-closure crisis (AACC); and systemic history, including topical or systemic medication use.
Identify abnormal pupillary function, an irregular pupil or a mid-dilated pupil.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A mid-dilated pupil may indicate a current or recent attack.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess conjunctival hyperemia; central and peripheral anterior chamber depth; inflammation; corneal swelling, diameter and endothelial cell loss; iris abnormalities; and lens changes, including cataract and glaukomflecken.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Conjunctival hyperemia, microcystic edema and stromal edema can occur in acute cases. Anterior chamber inflammation or a mid-dilated pupil may indicate a current or recent attack. A small corneal diameter indicates a smaller eye at greater risk for PACD.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess pressure at initial evaluation and after iridotomy.
Assess the chamber angle; after iridotomy, evaluate the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial examination; dark-room gonioscopy with compression/indentation after iridotomy if it was not performed immediately following the procedure.

diagnostic_workup.test: Fundus and optic nerve head evaluation
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the fundus and optic nerve head using direct ophthalmoscopy, slit-lamp biomicroscopy with an indirect lens, the central part of a gonioscopy lens, or retinal and optic nerve photography with a nonmydriatic camera through an undilated pupil.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial evaluation; repeat fundus examination after iridotomy when clinically indicated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Verify an opening by directly observing aqueous and pigment movement from the posterior to the anterior chamber; at follow-up, look for zonules, the anterior lens capsule or ciliary processes.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During iridotomy and at subsequent evaluation
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A red reflex alone does not establish patency.

follow_up.schedule: The document does not give a fixed interval after iridotomy. Patients with a residual open angle, or an open angle together with some PAS, should be examined at suitable intervals for increasing PAS.
recommended_tests: Confirm iridotomy patency by visualizing zonules, the anterior lens capsule or ciliary processes.
If not done immediately after iridotomy, perform dark-room gonioscopy with compression/indentation to assess the extent of PAS.
Examine the fundus when clinically indicated.
Monitor for increasing PAS in patients with a residual open angle or an open angle with some PAS.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Patients should learn the symptoms of AACC and be instructed to contact their ophthalmologist immediately if they occur. Patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness may be referred to vision rehabilitation and social services.

conditions.name: Primary Angle-Closure Suspect (PACS)
conditions.description: Iridotomy may be considered to lower the risk of developing angle closure.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: Patients who have not undergone iridotomy should be told about the potential for AACC and that some medicines may dilate the pupil and precipitate AACC.

conditions.name: acute angle-closure crisis (AACC)
conditions.description: An acute presentation for which the document advises initial medical lowering of IOP, followed by iridotomy as soon as possible.
conditions.epidemiology: Approximately half of fellow eyes can develop AACC within 5 years when the fellow eye has an anatomically narrow chamber angle.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Acute cases may show conjunctival hyperemia, microcystic edema or stromal edema. Anterior chamber inflammation or a mid-dilated pupil can suggest a current or recent attack.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess acute conjunctival and corneal findings, anterior chamber inflammation and pupil appearance.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Conjunctival hyperemia and corneal edema can occur in acute cases; inflammation or a mid-dilated pupil may suggest a current or recent attack.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess pressure before treatment and during perioperative care.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial evaluation and, if iridotomy is performed, immediately before surgery and within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify an anatomically narrow angle relevant to prophylactic iridotomy.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An anatomically narrow chamber angle is the stated criterion for scheduling fellow-eye prophylactic iridotomy.

recommended_tests: After iridotomy, check its patency and measure IOP.
Assess the extent of PAS with dark-room gonioscopy with compression/indentation if this was not done immediately after iridotomy.
Examine the fundus when clinically indicated.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Patients should be informed about AACC symptoms and instructed to contact their ophthalmologist immediately if symptoms develop.

conditions.name: plateau iris
conditions.description: The document discusses observation versus prophylactic iridoplasty for this condition but states that convincing evidence supporting prophylactic iridoplasty is lacking.

conditions.name: PAC
conditions.description: The document identifies PAC as a condition that may develop when IOP remains elevated over the long term after iridotomy.

follow_up.schedule: If IOP remains elevated long term and PAC develops, the document refers to follow-up procedures and intervals in the POAG PPP without specifying a separate PAC schedule.

conditions.name: PACG
conditions.description: The document identifies PACG as a condition that may develop when IOP remains elevated over the long term after iridotomy.

follow_up.schedule: If IOP remains elevated long term and PACG develops, the document refers to follow-up procedures and intervals in the POAG PPP without specifying a separate PACG schedule.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with POAG for whom IOP-lowering treatment is indicated.
decision_rules: Individualize the target IOP and revise it as the disease course warrants; the initial target should be at least 25% below pretreatment IOP.
A lower target IOP may be justified by more severe optic nerve damage, rapid progression, or other risk factors, including family history, age, or disc hemorrhages.
Select treatment by weighing adverse effects against effectiveness and tolerability. Medical treatment, laser therapy, incisional surgery, or combinations can lower IOP.

recommended_regimens.name: Medical therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: This is currently the most common initial approach to lowering IOP; select a regimen that achieves the desired reduction while balancing effectiveness and tolerability.

alternative_regimens.name: Laser trabeculoplasty
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used at the outset or added to existing POAG treatment to lower IOP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An initial or adjunctive IOP-lowering approach is appropriate.

alternative_regimens.name: Incisional surgery
alternative_regimens.summary: Can lower IOP, either on its own or together with other treatment.

response_assessment.method: Assess IOP against the individualized target and check ONH/RNFL and visual fields for stability.
response_assessment.interpretation: Progression despite target IOP calls for discussion of possible undetected IOP fluctuations, adherence, and treatment alternatives before lowering the target.

supportive_care: Assess patients receiving glaucoma medication for ocular and systemic adverse effects and toxicity.
Explain eyelid closure or nasolacrimal occlusion during topical medication use to limit systemic absorption.
Discuss the diagnosis, severity, prognosis, treatment plan, and possibility of lifelong therapy; encourage patients to report physical or emotional changes while taking glaucoma medications.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with POAG receiving laser treatment as an initial or adjunctive intervention.
decision_rules: Laser trabeculoplasty may be selected either as initial treatment or as an adjunct.
Before the procedure, confirm its indication and obtain informed consent after discussing risks, benefits, and anticipated outcomes.

recommended_regimens.name: Laser trabeculoplasty
recommended_regimens.summary: May be performed as initial or additional IOP-lowering treatment for POAG.

response_assessment.timepoint: Immediately before surgery and within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward
response_assessment.method: Check IOP at least once at each specified perioperative time.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 6 weeks after surgery, or sooner if IOP-related optic nerve damage is a concern

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document also states that Laser trabeculectomy lowers IOP and may be applied to 180 degrees or 360 degrees of the angle; it does not clarify the relationship between that named procedure and Laser trabeculoplasty.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with POAG undergoing incisional glaucoma surgery.
decision_rules: Perform preoperative gonioscopy, particularly when considering trabecular meshwork/Schlemm's canal-based MIGS.
Document the examination findings and surgical indication before proceeding, and obtain informed consent after reviewing risks, benefits, and expected outcomes.

recommended_regimens.name: Incisional glaucoma surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: An IOP-lowering surgical option that may be used alone or with other treatment.

response_assessment.timepoint: The first postoperative day and at least once during the first 1 to 2 weeks
response_assessment.method: Evaluate visual acuity, IOP, and the anterior segment.

response_assessment.timepoint: During a 3-month period after surgery, when complications are absent
response_assessment.method: Conduct additional visits assessing visual acuity, IOP, and the anterior segment.

response_assessment.timepoint: More frequently if postoperative complications arise
response_assessment.method: Assess for a flat or shallow anterior chamber, early bleb failure, increased inflammation, or Tenon's cyst.

supportive_care: Prescribe topical corticosteroids after surgery.

If bleb failure develops, use additional measures as needed to improve aqueous flow into the bleb and lower IOP, including injection of antifibrotic agents, bleb massage, suture adjustment, release or lysis, or bleb needling.
Address complications as they occur, including repair of a leaking bleb or reformation of a flat anterior chamber.
Explain that filtration surgery creates a lifelong risk of endophthalmitis; patients with pain and reduced vision together with redness and discharge should notify their ophthalmologist immediately.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with POAG undergoing follow-up, including those receiving topical ocular hyopotensive agents.
decision_rules: Consider changing treatment when target IOP is not reached and the expected benefit outweighs the risk, optic nerve damage progresses despite target IOP, the prescribed regimen is intolerable, or a medication becomes contraindicated.
If optic disc, imaging, or visual-field findings progress, the target pressure can be lowered. If the patient remains stable and needs or wants less medication, a higher target can be considered.
After prolonged optic nerve stability with low IOP during topical treatment, a carefully monitored reduction of medication may be appropriate.

response_assessment.method: Review interval ocular and systemic history, medication adverse effects and use, including the last administration; measure visual acuity and IOP, perform slit-lamp examination, and evaluate the ONH and visual field.
response_assessment.interpretation: Perform gonioscopy periodically and when an angle-closure component, anterior chamber shallowing, angle abnormality, or unexplained IOP change is suspected.

response_assessment.timepoint: Maximum interval of 6 months when target IOP is achieved, damage has not progressed, and control has lasted ≤6 months
Maximum interval of 12 months when target IOP is achieved, damage has not progressed, and control has lasted >6 months
Maximum interval of 1–2 months when damage progresses, whether or not target IOP is achieved
Maximum interval of 3–6 months when target IOP is not achieved but damage has not progressed

supportive_care: Explain the condition, treatment goals, current status, and relative benefits and risks of options so the patient can participate in planning.
Patients considering keratorefractive surgery should be told that laser vision correction can reduce contrast sensitivity and make IOP measurements less accurate.
Patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness can be referred to vision rehabilitation and social services and encouraged to use them.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: More advanced damage or greater lifetime risk from POAG may warrant evaluations more frequently than the stated maximum intervals.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Glaucoma suspect patients for whom IOP-lowering treatment is indicated, including an eye judged likely to progress to POAG.
decision_rules: Individualize the estimated target IOP and adjust it during the disease course when necessary.
When selecting treatment, balance the degree of IOP reduction against adverse effects and tolerability.
If one medication does not lower IOP sufficiently, switching to another medication as monotherapy or adding medication is appropriate until the desired IOP is reached.

recommended_regimens.name: Medical therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Currently the most common initial method of lowering IOP when treatment is chosen for a glaucoma suspect.

alternative_regimens.name: Alternative medication as monotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Switch medication if the initial medical treatment does not lower IOP sufficiently.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Insufficient IOP reduction with the current medication.

alternative_regimens.name: Additional medication
alternative_regimens.summary: Add medication to reach the desired IOP level.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Insufficient IOP reduction with the current medical treatment.

response_assessment.method: Measure IOP; look for structural changes in the optic disc and retina and functional change on visual-field testing.
response_assessment.interpretation: For newly detected glaucomatous visual-field damage in a glaucoma suspect, repeating the test is preferable. Consider perimetric and other structural information alongside digital imaging when making management decisions.

supportive_care: Explain eyelid closure or nasolacrimal occlusion after instilling medication to reduce systemic absorption.
Discuss risk factors, prognosis, life expectancy, the management plan, and the possibility that treatment, once begun, may continue long term.
Encourage patients taking glaucoma medication to report physical or emotional changes.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Glaucoma suspect patients undergoing follow-up, including patients receiving treatment.
decision_rules: Consider modifying treatment if target IOP is not reached and benefits outweigh risks, the regimen is intolerable, costs or other factors prevent adherence, or a new systemic condition or treatment could contraindicate current glaucoma therapy.
For a treated patient who has remained stable for a prolonged period without progression to POAG, cautious withdrawal of treatment may be considered.
If the patient converts to POAG, manage the patient under the POAG pathway.

response_assessment.method: Review interval ocular and systemic medical history and medications; for treated patients, ask about ocular medication adverse effects and use, including the time of the last dose. Measure visual acuity and IOP and perform slit-lamp examination.
response_assessment.interpretation: Gonioscopy is indicated for suspected development of an angle-closure component, anterior chamber shallowing, angle abnormalities, or an unexplained IOP change.

supportive_care: Explain the condition, its potential to develop into glaucoma, the reasons and goals for intervention, current status, and the benefits and risks of alternatives.
Patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness can be referred to vision rehabilitation and social services and encouraged to use them.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with PACS being considered for iridotomy.
decision_rules: Iridotomy may be considered to reduce the risk of developing angle closure.
A patient who has not undergone iridotomy should be advised about the potential for AACC and the possibility that medicines causing pupil dilation could induce AACC.

alternative_regimens.name: Iridotomy
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered to lower the risk of subsequent angle closure.

supportive_care: Explain the symptoms of AACC and advise immediate notification of the ophthalmologist if they occur.

decision_rules: First use medical treatment to reduce IOP, relieve pain, and clear corneal edema; then perform iridotomy as soon as possible.
Laser iridotomy is the preferred surgical treatment because of its favorable balance of benefit and risk.
Selection of cyclophotocoagulation rather than another procedure is left to the treating ophthalmologist in consultation with the patient.

recommended_regimens.name: Medical therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Use first during AACC to lower IOP, lessen pain, and clear corneal edema before iridotomy.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Before iridotomy, which should follow as soon as possible.

recommended_regimens.name: Laser iridotomy
recommended_regimens.summary: The preferred surgical intervention for AACC after initial medical treatment.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: As soon as possible after initial medical treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Cyclophotocoagulation
alternative_regimens.summary: Its selection over other procedures is a decision for the treating ophthalmologist and patient.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individualized consultation between the treating ophthalmologist and patient.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Anatomically narrow fellow eyes of patients with AACC.
decision_rules: Schedule prophylactic iridotomy for the fellow eye if its chamber angle is anatomically narrow.

recommended_regimens.name: Prophylactic iridotomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform in an anatomically narrow fellow eye because that eye is at risk of AACC.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Approximately half of fellow eyes can develop AACC within 5 years.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with plateau iris being considered for prophylactic iridoplasty.
decision_rules: Leave the choice between observation and treatment to the testing ophthalmologist: convincing evidence for prophylactic iridoplasty is lacking, and the procedure may cause pain and inflammation.

alternative_regimens.name: Iridoplasty
alternative_regimens.summary: Prophylactic use is an individualized option rather than an established preferred treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The testing ophthalmologist chooses treatment rather than observation after considering the uncertain evidence and possible pain and inflammation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not present observation or iridoplasty as uniformly preferable.

decision_rules: Confirm the need for surgery during preoperative evaluation and obtain informed consent after discussing risks, benefits, and expected outcomes.
Consider a parasympathomimetic before LPI to facilitate the procedure.
Use perioperative topical ocular hypotensive agents to prevent an abrupt IOP rise, especially in severe disease.
Verify patency by directly seeing aqueous and pigment move from the posterior to the anterior chamber; a red reflex by itself does not establish patency.
Enlarge the opening if necessary until its diameter is at least 100 microns.

response_assessment.timepoint: Immediately before iridotomy and within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward
response_assessment.method: Measure IOP at least once at each specified time.

Confirm patency by viewing zonules, the anterior lens capsule, or ciliary processes; measure IOP, assess the fundus when clinically indicated, and use dark-room gonisocopy with compression/indentation to assess PAS if this was not done immediately after iridotomy.

supportive_care: Prescribe topical corticosteroids after the procedure.
Ensure appropriate postoperative care.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients after iridotomy who have a residual open angle or both an open angle and some PAS, with or without glaucomatous optic neuropathy.
decision_rules: Arrange follow-up at intervals appropriate for detecting an increase in PAS.
If IOP remains elevated long term and PAC or PACG develops, ongoing medical IOP-lowering treatment may become necessary.

alternative_regimens.name: Medical therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Ongoing IOP-lowering medication may be needed after iridotomy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: IOP remains elevated long term and the patient develops PAC or PACG.

response_assessment.timepoint: At appropriate follow-up intervals after iridotomy
response_assessment.method: Check for increasing PAS and assess IOP.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistently elevated IOP with development of PAC or PACG may call for ongoing medical treatment.

supportive_care: Explain AACC symptoms and instruct patients to contact their ophthalmologist immediately if symptoms develop.
Patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness can be referred to vision rehabilitation and social services and encouraged to use them.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For ongoing IOP treatment when PAC or PACG develops, the document refers to POAG PPP follow-up procedures and intervals.

artifacts.title: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma initial evaluation
artifacts.description: History: Review ocular history, including refractive error, trauma and previous surgery; race/ethnicity; family and systemic history; relevant records; current medications; and prior glaucoma laser or incisional surgery. Examination: Measure visual acuity and IOP; assess pupils, confrontation visual fields, the anterior segment by slit lamp, the angle by gonioscopy, ONH, RNFL and the fundus. Diagnostic testing: Measure CCT, evaluate visual fields, and obtain ONH, RNFL and macular imaging.
artifacts.summary: This checklist brings together the history, examination and testing elements specified for an initial POAG evaluation.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It identifies the information used to assess glaucoma and establish a basis for subsequent management.

artifacts.title: Laser trabeculoplasty perioperative responsibilities
artifacts.source_heading: Perioperative Care for Laser Trabeculoplasty Patients
artifacts.description: The operating ophthalmologist obtains informed consent after discussing surgical risks, benefits and expected outcomes; confirms the indication through preoperative evaluation; checks IOP at least once immediately before surgery and within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward; and arranges an examination within 6 weeks, or earlier if IOP-related optic nerve damage is a concern.
artifacts.summary: This checklist specifies the consent, assessment, IOP measurement and follow-up duties surrounding laser trabeculoplasty.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It sets out perioperative checks and the timing of early postoperative review.

artifacts.title: Incisional glaucoma surgery perioperative responsibilities
artifacts.source_heading: Perioperative Care in Incisional Glaucoma Surgery Patients
artifacts.description: Before surgery, the operating ophthalmologist performs gonioscopy, particularly if considering trabecular meshwork/Schlemm's canal-based MIGS; obtains informed consent after explaining risks, benefits and expected outcomes; and documents the findings and surgical indications. After surgery, prescribe topical corticosteroids; assess visual acuity, IOP and the anterior segment on the first postoperative day and at least once during the first 1 to 2 weeks; and, if there are no complications, make further assessments during a 3-month period. Increase visit frequency for a flat or shallow anterior chamber, early bleb failure, increased inflammation or Tenon's cyst. If bleb failure emerges, consider measures needed to improve flow into the bleb and reduce IOP, including antifibrotic injection, bleb massage, suture adjustment, release or lysis, or bleb needling. Treat complications as they arise, including bleb leakage or a flat anterior chamber. Explain the lifelong risk of endophthalmitis after filtration surgery and the need for immediate ophthalmologist notification if pain and reduced vision occur with redness and discharge.
artifacts.summary: This checklist covers preoperative assessment, postoperative visits, bleb-related interventions, complication management and patient warning signs.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports postoperative surveillance and timely action when complications develop.

artifacts.title: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma follow-up evaluation
artifacts.description: History: Obtain interval ocular and systemic history, ask about ocular medication adverse effects, and review relevant medication use and the time of the last dose. Examination: Measure visual acuity and IOP, perform slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and assess ONH and visual fields. Perform gonioscopy periodically and when an angle-closure component, anterior chamber shallowing, an angle abnormality or an unexplained IOP change is suspected.
artifacts.summary: This checklist identifies the history and examination components of POAG follow-up.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports assessment of disease status, treatment effects and possible changes in the anterior chamber angle.

artifacts.title: Consensus-based Guidelines for Follow-up Glaucoma Status
artifacts.description: IOP means intraocular pressure, and NA means not applicable. The listed intervals are the maximum recommended time between evaluations; more advanced damage or greater lifetime risk from primary open-angle glaucoma may warrant more frequent visits.
artifacts.summary: The table relates target IOP attainment, damage progression and duration of control to an approximate follow-up interval.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It provides consensus-based maximum intervals for scheduling glaucoma reassessment while allowing closer surveillance when risk is greater.

artifacts.title: Glaucoma suspect initial evaluation
artifacts.description: History: Review ocular history, including refractive error, trauma and previous ocular surgery; race/ethnicity; family and systemic history; relevant records; current and previous ocular and nonocular medications; and prior cataract surgery, LASIK or incisional surgery. Examination: Measure visual acuity and IOP; examine pupils, confrontation visual fields, the anterior segment by slit lamp, the angle by gonioscopy, ONH, RNFL and the fundus. Diagnostic testing: Measure CCT, evaluate visual fields, and obtain ONH, RNFL and macular imaging. Repeating visual-field testing is best when glaucomatous field damage is newly found in a glaucoma suspect; consider perimetric and other structural findings alongside digital imaging when making management decisions.
artifacts.summary: This checklist assembles the initial assessment elements presented for a glaucoma suspect.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports evaluation of suspected glaucoma and cautions against basing management decisions on imaging alone.

artifacts.title: Glaucoma suspect follow-up evaluation
artifacts.description: History: Review interval ocular and systemic medical history and medications. If the patient is treated, ask about ocular medication adverse effects and review medication use, including the time of the last administration. Examination: Measure visual acuity and IOP and perform slit-lamp biomicroscopy. Gonioscopy is indicated if an angle-closure component is suspected, the anterior chamber becomes shallow, an angle abnormality is present or IOP changes without explanation.
artifacts.summary: This checklist identifies follow-up history and examination elements for a glaucoma suspect.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports monitoring of ocular status and treatment effects and identifies circumstances calling for gonioscopy.

artifacts.title: Primary Angle-Closure Disease initial evaluation
artifacts.source_heading: Primary Angle-Closure Disease (Initial Evaluation and Therapy)
artifacts.description: History: Ask about blurred vision, halos, eye pain, headache and redness; family history of AACC; and systemic history, including topical or systemic medication use. Examination: Assess refractive status, pupils, IOP and the angle by gonioscopy. Slit-lamp assessment includes conjunctival hyperemia; central and peripheral anterior chamber depth; anterior chamber inflammation; corneal swelling, diameter and endothelial cell loss; iris atrophy, posterior synechiae, pupillary function and shape; and lens findings such as cataract and glaukomflecken. Evaluate the fundus and optic nerve head using the examination or imaging approaches described in the guideline. Diagnostic testing includes anterior segment imaging, ocular biometry and provocative testing.
artifacts.summary: This checklist combines the history, ocular findings and diagnostic tests specified for an initial PACD evaluation.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It directs attention to findings associated with angle closure and a recent or current acute attack.

artifacts.title: Iridotomy perioperative responsibilities
artifacts.description: The operating ophthalmologist obtains informed consent after discussing risks, benefits and expected outcomes and confirms the need for surgery preoperatively. Consider a preoperative parasympathomimetic to facilitate LPI. Use perioperative topical ocular hypotensive agents to prevent an abrupt IOP rise, particularly in severe disease. Confirm iridotomy patency by directly observing aqueous and pigment move from the posterior to the anterior chamber; a red reflex alone does not establish patency. Enlarge the opening as needed to a diameter of at least 100 microns. Check IOP at least once immediately before surgery and within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward, prescribe postoperative topical corticosteroids and provide adequate postoperative care.
artifacts.summary: This checklist covers consent, preparation, prevention of IOP elevation, confirmation of patency and postoperative care for iridotomy.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It specifies how to verify an effective opening and monitor for an early pressure rise.

artifacts.title: Assessment after iridotomy
artifacts.source_heading: Primary Angle-Closure Disease (Initial Evaluation and Therapy) (continued)
artifacts.description: At follow-up, verify iridotomy patency by observing zonules, the anterior lens capsule or ciliary processes, and measure IOP. If it was not done immediately after iridotomy, use dark-room gonisocopy with compression/indentation to assess the extent of PAS. Examine the fundus when clinically indicated.
artifacts.summary: This checklist lists the follow-up assessments specified after iridotomy.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It supports confirmation of patency and evaluation of IOP and peripheral anterior synechiae.

recommendations.statement: At the initial evaluation, obtain the ocular, systemic, family, and medication histories; document race/ethnicity and any prior glaucoma laser or incisional surgery; and review pertinent records.
Measure visual acuity and IOP; examine the pupils, confrontation visual fields, anterior segment, ONH, RNFL, and fundus; and perform gonioscopy.
Measure CCT, assess the visual field, and obtain ONH, RNFL, and macular imaging.
Aim to keep IOP within an individualized target range while maintaining stable ONH, RNFL, and visual-field findings. Reassess the target over the course of the disease.

recommendations.source_heading: Management Plan for Patients in Whom Therapy is Indicated

recommendations.statement: Set the initial target IOP at least 25% below pretreatment IOP. A lower target may be warranted with more severe optic nerve injury, rapid progression, or other risk factors such as family history, age, or disc hemorrhages.
recommendations.source_heading: Management Plan for Patients in Whom Therapy is Indicated

recommendations.statement: Lower IOP with medication, laser therapy, incisional surgery, or a combination. When selecting medical therapy, weigh effectiveness against adverse effects to achieve the desired IOP reduction with a tolerable regimen.
recommendations.context: Medical treatment is described as the most common initial IOP-lowering intervention.
recommendations.source_heading: Management Plan for Patients in Whom Therapy is Indicated

recommendations.statement: If damage progresses despite IOP being at target, discuss possible unrecognized IOP variation, adherence, and alternative treatments before lowering the target IOP.
recommendations.source_heading: Management Plan for Patients in Whom Therapy is Indicated

recommendations.statement: Assess patients taking glaucoma medication for ocular and systemic adverse effects and toxicity.
recommendations.source_heading: Management Plan for Patients in Whom Therapy is Indicated

recommendations.statement: Laser trabeculoplasty may be used as initial treatment or as an adjunct.
recommendations.source_heading: Management Plan for Patients in Whom Therapy is Indicated

recommendations.statement: Before laser trabeculoplasty, confirm the indication at the preoperative evaluation and obtain informed consent after discussing expected outcomes, benefits, and risks with the patient or surrogate decision maker.
recommendations.source_heading: Perioperative Care for Laser Trabeculoplasty Patients

recommendations.statement: Check IOP at least once immediately before laser trabeculoplasty and again within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward.
recommendations.source_heading: Perioperative Care for Laser Trabeculoplasty Patients

recommendations.statement: Examine the patient within 6 weeks after laser trabeculoplasty, or earlier if IOP-related optic nerve injury is a concern.
recommendations.source_heading: Perioperative Care for Laser Trabeculoplasty Patients

recommendations.statement: Perform preoperative gonioscopy, particularly when considering trabecular meshwork/Schlemm's canal-based MIGS.
recommendations.source_heading: Perioperative Care in Incisional Glaucoma Surgery Patients

recommendations.statement: Obtain informed consent after discussing surgical risks, benefits, and expected outcomes with the patient or surrogate decision maker, and ensure the preoperative evaluation documents the findings and surgical indications accurately.
recommendations.context: Responsibilities of the operating ophthalmologist in incisional surgery.
recommendations.source_heading: Perioperative Care in Incisional Glaucoma Surgery Patients

recommendations.statement: Prescribe topical corticosteroids after incisional glaucoma surgery.
recommendations.source_heading: Perioperative Care in Incisional Glaucoma Surgery Patients

recommendations.statement: Assess visual acuity, IOP, and the anterior segment on the first postoperative day and at least once during the first 1 to 2 weeks. If there are no complications, arrange further visits during a 3-month period to reassess these findings.
recommendations.source_heading: Perioperative Care in Incisional Glaucoma Surgery Patients

recommendations.statement: Increase follow-up frequency as needed when postoperative complications arise, including a flat or shallow anterior chamber, early bleb failure, increased inflammation, or a Tenon's cyst.

If bleb failure becomes evident, use additional measures as needed to improve aqueous flow into the bleb and lower IOP; options include antifibrotic injections, bleb massage, suture adjustment, release or lysis, and bleb needling.
Treat postoperative complications as they occur, including repairing a leaking bleb or reforming a flat anterior chamber.
Explain the lifelong risk of endophthalmitis after filtration surgery and instruct the patient to notify the ophthalmologist immediately if pain and reduced vision occur with redness and discharge.
Discuss the diagnosis, disease severity, prognosis, treatment plan, and likelihood of lifelong treatment with patients receiving medical therapy.

recommendations.statement: Teach eyelid closure or nasolacrimal occlusion during topical medication use to limit systemic absorption, and encourage patients to report physical or emotional changes while taking glaucoma medications.
recommendations.rationale: Eyelid closure or nasolacrimal occlusion is intended to reduce systemic absorption.
recommendations.source_heading: Patient Education for Patients with Medical Therapy

recommendations.statement: At follow-up, obtain interval ocular and systemic histories, ask about ocular-medication adverse effects, and review relevant medication use, including the time of the most recent dose.
At follow-up, measure visual acuity and IOP, perform slit-lamp examination, and evaluate the ONH and visual field.
Repeat gonioscopy periodically and when an angle-closure component, anterior chamber shallowing, an anterior chamber angle abnormality, or an unexplained IOP change is suspected.

Consider changing treatment when target IOP is not reached and the expected benefits outweigh the risks, when optic nerve injury progresses despite target IOP, when the prescribed regimen is not tolerated, or when a medication becomes contraindicated.
A carefully monitored reduction in topical ocular hypotensive treatment may be appropriate after a prolonged period of stable optic nerve findings and low IOP.

The target pressure may be lowered if optic disc, imaging, or visual-field findings progress. A higher target may be considered when the patient remains stable and needs or wishes to use less medication.
Explain the disease, treatment rationale and goals, current disease status, and comparative benefits and risks of alternatives so patients can participate in planning their care.
Tell patients considering keratorefractive surgery that laser vision correction may reduce contrast sensitivity and make IOP measurements less accurate.
Consider referral to vision rehabilitation and social services, and encourage their use, for patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness.
When target IOP has been achieved without damage progression, use a maximum follow-up interval of 6 months if control has lasted ≤6 months, or 12 months if control has lasted >6 months.

recommendations.statement: Use a maximum follow-up interval of 1–2 months when damage is progressing, whether or not target IOP has been achieved. When target IOP has not been achieved but damage is not progressing, use a maximum interval of 3–6 months.
recommendations.source_heading: Consensus-based Guidelines for Follow-up Glaucoma Status

recommendations.statement: Evaluate more frequently when more advanced damage or greater lifetime risk warrants it.

Discuss the number and severity of risk factors, prognosis, life expectancy, management plan, and possibility that treatment, once begun, will continue long term.

Warn patients with PAS who have not undergone iridotomy about AACC risk and the possibility that pupil-dilating medicines could trigger it.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: The Academy’s Preferred Practice Pattern® (PPP) benchmarks are intended to give practitioners clinically useful, sufficiently specific guidance. Each recommendation is meant to receive separate ratings for its importance to care and the strength of its supporting evidence. The guidance addresses usual patterns of practice rather than every individual circumstance: it may not suit every patient, guarantee a favorable outcome, encompass every reasonable approach, or rule out other appropriate care. Physicians retain responsibility for decisions based on each patient’s circumstances. The American Academy of Ophthalmology offers members help with ethical questions arising in ophthalmic practice. These guidelines are not mandatory standards for individual cases, and the Academy disclaims liability for claims arising from their use. For each major condition, the guidance summarizes history, examination, ancillary testing, management, follow-up, and patient education. Each PPP draws on a search of English-language articles in PubMed and the Cochrane Library; an expert panel reviews the findings and rates evidence strength when sufficient evidence is available. Individual studies are rated using a scale based on the Scottish Intercollegiate Guideline Network (SIGN): I++ denotes high-quality meta-analyses or systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), or RCTs with very low bias risk; I+ denotes well-conducted versions of those studies with low bias risk; I– denotes versions with high bias risk. II++ covers high-quality systematic reviews of case-control or cohort studies, or high-quality individual studies with very low confounding or bias risk and a high probability of causality. II+ covers well-conducted case-control or cohort studies with low confounding or bias risk and a moderate probability of causality. II– covers such studies with high confounding or bias risk and a significant possibility that the association is not causal. III covers nonanalytic evidence, such as case reports or case series.

document_sections.heading: Introduction (continued)
document_sections.content: Care recommendations are based on the overall evidence. Under Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE), Good quality (GQ) means further research is very unlikely to alter confidence in the effect estimate; Moderate quality (MQ) means further research is likely to affect confidence substantially and may change the estimate; Insufficient quality (IQ) means further research is very likely to affect confidence substantially and probably change an estimate that remains highly uncertain. A Strong recommendation (SR) applies when desirable effects clearly outweigh undesirable effects, or clearly do not. A Discretionary recommendation (DR) applies when the balance is less certain because evidence quality is low or benefits and harms appear closely balanced. PPPs emphasize technical guidance, but their application should put patients’ needs first. The AAO offers members assistance with ethical dilemmas arising in practice, as described in the AAO Code of Ethics.

document_sections.heading: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (Initial Evaluation)
document_sections.content: This part addresses initial assessment, treatment planning, procedural care, and education for patients with primary open-angle glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: Initial Exam History (Key elements)
document_sections.content: Obtain ocular history, including refractive error, trauma, and previous ocular operations; race/ethnicity; family and systemic histories; relevant prior records; current medications; and any earlier glaucoma laser treatment or incisional surgery.

document_sections.heading: Initial Physical Exam (Key elements)
document_sections.content: Measure visual acuity and IOP; assess pupils, confrontation visual fields, the optic nerve head (ONH), retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL), and fundus; and perform slit-lamp biomicroscopy and gonioscopy.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Testing (Key elements)
document_sections.content: Measure central corneal thickness (CCT), evaluate visual fields, and obtain ONH, RNFL, and macular imaging.

document_sections.heading: Management Plan for Patients in Whom Therapy is Indicated
document_sections.content: Treatment aims to keep IOP within an individualized target range while maintaining stable ONH/RNFL findings and visual fields. Reassess and adjust the estimated target as the disease evolves. Initially, aim for pressure at least 25% below pretreatment IOP; more severe optic nerve injury, rapid progression, or other risk factors such as family history, age, or disc hemorrhages can justify a lower target. Medical treatment, laser treatment, and incisional surgery can lower IOP, individually or together. Medication is currently the most common initial intervention; choose a regimen that balances efficacy and adverse effects to achieve the desired reduction with the greatest feasible effectiveness and tolerance. Table 4 of the POAG PPP provides an overview of options. If disease advances despite target pressure, discuss potentially missed IOP fluctuations, adherence, and treatment alternatives before lowering the target. Check patients receiving glaucoma medications for ocular and systemic toxicity and adverse effects. Laser trabeculoplasty may serve as initial or additional POAG treatment; Table 5 of the POAG PPP is referenced. The document states that laser trabeculectomy lowers IOP effectively and may treat 180 degrees or 360 degrees of the angle.

document_sections.heading: Perioperative Care for Laser Trabeculoplasty Patients
document_sections.content: The operating ophthalmologist should discuss surgical risks, benefits, and expected outcomes before obtaining consent from the patient or surrogate; confirm the indication through preoperative assessment; check IOP at least once immediately before treatment and again within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward; and arrange an examination within 6 weeks, earlier if IOP-related optic nerve injury is a concern.

document_sections.heading: Perioperative Care in Incisional Glaucoma Surgery Patients
document_sections.content: The operating ophthalmologist should perform preoperative gonioscopy, particularly when considering trabecular meshwork/Schlemm's canal-based MIGS, for which Table 6 of the POAG PPP is referenced. Discuss expected results, benefits, and risks before obtaining patient or surrogate consent, and document the preoperative findings and surgical indication accurately. Prescribe postoperative topical corticosteroids. Evaluate visual acuity, IOP, and the anterior segment on the first postoperative day and at least once during the first 1 to 2 weeks. Without complications, arrange further assessments of those findings during a 3-month period.

document_sections.heading: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (Initial Evaluation) (continued)
document_sections.content: After incisional surgery, increase visit frequency as needed for a flat or shallow anterior chamber, early bleb failure, greater inflammation, or a Tenon's cyst. If the bleb begins to fail, use additional measures as needed to promote aqueous entry and reduce IOP; listed options are antifibrotic injection, bleb massage, suture adjustment, suture release or lysis, and bleb needling. Address complications as they arise, including repair of a leaking bleb or reformation of a flat anterior chamber. Explain that filtration surgery creates a lifelong risk of endophthalmitis and instruct patients to contact their ophthalmologist immediately if pain and reduced vision occur with redness and discharge.

document_sections.heading: Patient Education for Patients with Medical Therapy
document_sections.content: Discuss the diagnosis, disease severity, outlook, care plan, and likelihood of lifelong treatment. Teach eyelid closure or nasolacrimal occlusion with topical medication to limit systemic absorption. Ask patients to report physical or emotional changes while taking glaucoma medications.

document_sections.heading: Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (Follow-up Evaluation)
document_sections.content: This part addresses interval assessment, possible treatment changes, education, and follow-up timing in primary open-angle glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Exam History
document_sections.content: Review ocular and systemic events since the previous visit, adverse effects of ocular drugs, and relevant medication use, including when the last dose was given.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Physical Exam
document_sections.content: Measure visual acuity and IOP, perform slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and evaluate the ONH and visual field. Perform gonioscopy periodically and when an angle-closure component, a shallower anterior chamber, an angle abnormality, or an unexplained IOP change is suspected.

document_sections.heading: Adjustment of Therapy
document_sections.content: Consider changing treatment when target IOP is unmet and expected benefits exceed risks; when optic nerve injury progresses despite target IOP; when the patient cannot tolerate the prescribed regimen; or when a contraindication to a medication develops. If the optic nerve remains stable and IOP stays low for a prolonged period during topical ocular hyopotensive treatment, a carefully monitored reduction in medication may be appropriate. Progressive optic disc, imaging, or visual-field changes can warrant lowering the target pressure. Raising the target may be considered for a stable patient who needs or wants less medication.

document_sections.heading: Patient Education
document_sections.content: Explain the disease, treatment rationale and goals, current status, and comparative benefits and risks of alternatives so patients can participate meaningfully in planning care. Tell patients considering keratorefractive surgery that laser vision correction may reduce contrast sensitivity and make IOP measurements less accurate. Patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness may be referred to, and encouraged to use, suitable vision rehabilitation and social services.

document_sections.heading: Follow-Up:
document_sections.content: Consensus-based Guidelines for Follow-up Glaucoma Status sets maximum recommended evaluation intervals according to whether target IOP has been achieved, whether damage is progressing, and how long control has lasted. Patients with more advanced injury or greater lifetime risk from primary open-angle glaucoma may need assessment more often.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Evaluation)
document_sections.content: This section describes initial assessment, treatment decisions, follow-up, and education for a patient suspected of having glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: Initial Exam History (Key elements)
document_sections.content: Record ocular history, including refractive error, trauma, and earlier eye surgery; race/ethnicity; family and systemic histories; relevant records; current and past ocular and nonocular medications; and prior cataract surgery, LASIK, and/or incisional surgery.

document_sections.heading: Initial Physical Exam (Key elements)
document_sections.content: Measure visual acuity and IOP; assess pupils, confrontation visual fields, the ONH, RNFL, and fundus; and perform slit-lamp biomicroscopy and gonioscopy.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Testing (Key elements)
document_sections.content: Measure CCT and assess visual fields. When glaucomatous visual-field injury is newly found in a glaucoma suspect, repeating the test is preferable. Obtain ONH, RNFL, and macular imaging, but base management decisions on all perimetric and other structural findings as well as digital imaging.

document_sections.heading: Management Plan for Patients in Whom Therapy is Indicated
document_sections.content: For an eye likely to progress to POAG, monitor IOP or lower it with treatment, watch for structural changes in the optic disc and retina, and assess visual fields for functional optic nerve changes. Several circumstances may prompt treatment of a glaucoma suspect; the POAG Suspect PPP provides further considerations. Individualize the estimated target IOP and revise it as disease evolves. Medication is currently the most common initial means of reducing IOP; weigh effectiveness against adverse effects to choose a maximally effective, tolerable regimen that achieves the intended reduction. Table 2 of the POAG Suspect PPP surveys available options. If medication does not lower IOP sufficiently, either substitute another drug as monotherapy or add medication until the desired IOP is reached.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Exam History
document_sections.content: Review interim ocular history and systemic illnesses and medications. For treated patients, ask about ocular-drug adverse effects and relevant medication use, including the time of the most recent dose.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Physical Exam
document_sections.content: Measure visual acuity and IOP and perform slit-lamp biomicroscopy. Gonioscopy is indicated if development of an angle-closure component, anterior chamber shallowing, an angle abnormality, or an otherwise unexplained IOP change is suspected.

document_sections.heading: Adjustment of Therapy
document_sections.content: Reasons to reconsider therapy include failure to reach target IOP when benefits of a change outweigh risks; inability to tolerate the prescribed regimen; nonadherence because of cost or other factors; new systemic illness or treatment that may contraindicate current glaucoma therapy; or conversion to POAG, for which the Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma PPP is referenced. If a treated patient remains stable without progression to POAG for a prolonged period, cautious treatment withdrawal may be considered.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Evaluation) (continued)
document_sections.content: This continuation addresses education for patients suspected of having glaucoma.

document_sections.heading: Patient Education
document_sections.content: Discuss the number and severity of risk factors, prognosis, life expectancy, care plan, and likelihood that treatment, once begun, may continue long term. Explain the condition’s potential to become glaucoma, its present status, the aims and reasons for intervention, and the relative advantages and risks of alternatives. Teach eyelid closure or nasolacrimal occlusion after instilling medication to reduce systemic uptake. Ask patients to notify their ophthalmologist about physical or emotional changes while using glaucoma medication. Patients with substantial vision loss or blindness may be referred to, and encouraged to use, appropriate vision rehabilitation and social services.

document_sections.heading: Primary Angle-Closure Disease (Initial Evaluation and Therapy)
document_sections.content: This part covers initial evaluation, iridotomy-related decisions and care, follow-up, and education in primary angle-closure disease.

document_sections.heading: Initial Exam History (Key elements)
document_sections.content: Ask about ocular symptoms and history, including blurred vision, halos around lights, eye pain, headache, and redness; family history of acute angle-closure crisis (AACC); and systemic history, including topical or systemic medication use.

document_sections.heading: Initial Physical Exam (Key elements)
document_sections.content: Assess refractive status and pupils. On slit-lamp examination, look for conjunctival redness in acute cases; narrowing of central and peripheral anterior chamber depth; inflammation suggesting a present or recent attack; and corneal swelling, including microcystic or stromal edema, which is common acutely. A small corneal diameter suggests a smaller eye at greater PACD risk. Assess diffuse or localized iris atrophy, posterior synechiae, altered pupil function or shape, and a mid-dilated pupil, which can suggest a current or recent attack. Examine for cataract, glaukomflecken, and corneal endothelial cell loss. Measure IOP and perform gonioscopy. Evaluate the fundus and optic nerve head with a direct ophthalmoscope, slit-lamp biomicroscope and indirect lens, the central part of a gonioscopy lens, or nonmydriatic photography through an undilated pupil.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Testing (Key elements)
document_sections.content: Diagnostic options listed are anterior segment imaging, ocular biometry, and provocative testing.

document_sections.heading: Management Plan for Patients in Whom Iridotomy is Indicated
document_sections.content: In Primary Angle-Closure Suspect (PACS), iridotomy may be considered to lower the risk of angle closure. During AACC, first use medication to reduce IOP, relieve pain, and clear corneal edema, then perform iridotomy as soon as possible; Table 4 of the POAG PPP is referenced. Laser iridotomy is the preferred surgical approach for AACC because its benefits and risks compare favorably. Warn patients with PACS who have not undergone iridotomy about AACC risk and the possibility that medicines causing pupil dilation could precipitate it. The treating ophthalmologist and patient should decide whether to select cyclophotocoagulation rather than another procedure. Schedule prophylactic iridotomy for an anatomically narrow fellow-eye angle: approximately half of fellow eyes can develop AACC within 5 years. Convincing evidence supporting preventive iridoplasty in plateau iris is lacking, and the procedure can cause pain and inflammation; the testing ophthalmologist should decide whether to observe or treat.

document_sections.heading: Perioperative Care for Iridotomy Patients
document_sections.content: The operating ophthalmologist should explain anticipated outcomes, benefits, and risks before obtaining patient or surrogate consent and confirm the surgical need preoperatively. Consider a parasympathomimetic before LPI. Use perioperative topical ocular hypotensive agents to prevent an abrupt IOP rise, especially in severe disease. Confirm iridotomy patency by directly seeing aqueous and pigment move from the posterior to anterior chamber; a red reflex alone does not establish patency. Enlarge the opening when needed to reach at least 100 microns in diameter. Check IOP at least once immediately before surgery and within 30 minutes to 2 hours afterward, prescribe postoperative topical corticosteroids, and ensure adequate postoperative care.

document_sections.heading: Primary Angle-Closure Disease (Initial Evaluation and Therapy) (continued)
document_sections.content: At follow-up after iridotomy, verify patency by seeing the zonules, anterior lens capsule, or ciliary processes, and measure IOP. If not performed immediately after iridotomy, use dark-room gonisocopy with compression/indentation to determine the extent of peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS). Examine the fundus when clinically indicated.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up of Patients after Iridotomy
document_sections.content: Whether or not glaucomatous optic neuropathy is present, follow patients who retain an open angle or an open angle with some PAS at suitable intervals to detect increasing PAS. Persistently elevated IOP with subsequent PAC or PACG may require continuing IOP-lowering medication; the POAG PPP is referenced for follow-up procedures and intervals.

document_sections.heading: Patient Education
document_sections.content: Warn patients with PAS who have not undergone iridotomy about possible AACC and medicines that may dilate the pupil and trigger a crisis. Explain AACC symptoms and instruct patients to contact their ophthalmologist immediately if they occur. Patients with substantial visual impairment or blindness may be referred to, and encouraged to use, suitable vision rehabilitation and social services.
